R Coding Project, Digital Literacy in South Bend

ITAO 20200: Foundations of Statistics

J. S. Akosa, F. Bilson Darku, J. Waddell


The city of South Bend conducted its first Digital Literacy survey in 2022. Nearly 300 residents rated their own proficiency in the digital realm on tasks such as

  • sending and receiving emails;
  • downloading and managing digital content;
  • using the search command to locate files on a device;
  • videoconferencing;
  • streaming content, such as videos or podcasts;
  • doing online banking or shopping;
  • using word processing, spreadsheet, or presentation tools.

Each skill was rated on a scale from 1 to 5, with higher scores indicating greater self-reported proficiency. Respondents also provided demographic information, such as gender, age, income, and education, that can be used to group their scores.

The data set has been cleaned and is ready for analysis. Your task is to perform the analyses described in this guide in R and then use your output to answer questions that show your understanding of the results.

A Starter Code R script file has been created for you. It contains code that a) reads in the data and b) performs some data management. After you read through and run that code, you will write your own code to analyze the data, following the directions in this guide.

You may not use AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, or Gemini) to write any of your code. Any indication that your code was produced by an AI tool will be treated as an honor code violation.

When you have finished writing your code, you must compile your results into a report. A compiled report combines the code you wrote with the output it produced. The compiled report is a required part of the coding project, and you will upload it to Canvas for grading.

Most of the points on the coding project come from the questions on WebAssign, which ask you to interpret the output you generated (much like the questions on an in-class assignment or a homework assignment). Your answers should be based on your own understanding of the analyses you performed.

Unlike on a homework assignment or an ICA, the green checkmarks and red x’s are turned off for this assignment. You may work with other people, but each person must a) write their own code, b) submit their own compiled report, and c) answer their own WebAssign questions based on their own analysis.

Getting Started

  1. Open the R Coding Project, Digital Literacy in South Bend assignment on WebAssign. The first question contains a link called R Project Starter Code, Digital Literacy Data. Click on the link, and the Starter Code will open in a new browser tab. Select all of the code and copy it.

  2. If you are working on a classroom computer, start Google Drive for desktop from the Start menu. Then open your ITAO 20200 R Project, which is saved in your ITAO 20200 R Project folder on your Google Drive (G: drive).

    Be sure that your ITAO 20200 R Project is open. This is a very important step. If you do not open your project from your G: drive, your work will be saved only on the computer you are using. If that computer has a problem, or someone else is using it when you return to the classroom, you will not be able to get to the work you have already completed.

    If your project is not open, use the dropdown menu in the top right-hand corner of RStudio and choose “Open Project…”

    Then, navigate through the G: drive to your ITAO 20200 R Project folder. Your R project file has an icon that looks like this: . You may also see a .Rproj extension at the end of its name. Click on this file to open your project before going on to the next step.

  3. Open a new R Script window. To do this, find the dropdown menu with a white plus sign inside a green circle (top left-hand side of RStudio) and choose the first option, R Script.

  4. Paste the Starter Code you copied in step i into this new script. Then save the file by going to File > Save As… (You can also click the save icon at the top of the screen or use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl + S.) Name the file R Coding Project YourLastName, replacing YourLastName with your own last name. Do not use any punctuation in your file name.

  5. Read through the first 45 lines of the Starter Code. These lines import the data, perform some data management tasks (such as shortening some variable names and putting the groups of some variables in a logical order), and load the packages needed for the analyses.

    Once you understand what these lines do, select and run the first 45 lines of code. Run these lines only once. Do not copy these commands into your own code; they have already been done for you.

    If you receive an error saying that a package (such as car) is not installed, install the package and then run the library line again.

  6. Read through the Required Analyses section of this guide. Each step there matches a numbered section of the Starter Code.

  7. Write your own code in the matching space in your Starter Code file, following the directions in the Required Analyses section. Put each piece of code in its designated spot. This will make it easier to find your output when you answer the WebAssign questions. Remember that you may not use AI tools to write your code.

  8. Save your Starter Code file often while you work, and again when you finish. If you do not finish the project in one sitting, you can open the file later and continue where you left off.

  9. When all of your code is complete, compile your report as an HTML file, following the instructions at the end of this guide. The compiled report is saved in the same folder as your Starter Code file. As long as you are working in your ITAO 20200 R Project (step ii), your report will be saved on your G: drive, where you can open it from any computer. Use your compiled report to answer the questions in the R Coding Project assignment on WebAssign.

  10. The ITAO 20200 professors recommend that you use the Mendoza classroom computers to complete your coding project. Mendoza’s IT staff keeps these machines up to date with the latest version of R; computers in other university spaces may not be up to date.

Required Analyses

Assume \(\alpha =0.05\) for all analyses.

  1. Descriptive statistics. For each variable below, generate descriptive statistics that include at least the sample size, mean, and standard deviation. You will need all three to answer the WebAssign questions.

  1. Collaboration;

  2. Safe_online_practices;

  3. SearchInternet for each level of Gender;

  4. Online_shopping for each level of Income;

  5. WordProcessing for each level of Education;

  6. Total_Percent_Score for each level of Age.

Use the base R commands shown below. Each example uses a variable that is not part of this project (Online_banking), so you will need to replace the variable names with the ones listed above.

For a single variable (parts a and b), use the c() command. Every line refers to the same variable:

c(n      = length(digital$Online_banking),
  mean   = round(mean(digital$Online_banking), 2),
  sd     = round(sd(digital$Online_banking), 2),
  median = round(median(digital$Online_banking), 2),
  min    = min(digital$Online_banking),
  max    = max(digital$Online_banking),
  se     = round(sd(digital$Online_banking) / sqrt(length(digital$Online_banking)), 2))

For a variable broken down by group (parts c through f), use the by() command. The first item is the quantitative variable (the dependent variable, or DV), and the second item is the categorical grouping variable (the independent variable, or IV). The function(x) part applies the same calculations to each group, so you do not change the x’s inside it; you change only the two variable names on the first line.

by(digital$Online_banking, digital$Housing_situation, function(x) {
  c(n      = length(x),
    mean   = round(mean(x), 2),
    sd     = round(sd(x), 2),
    median = round(median(x), 2),
    min    = min(x),
    max    = max(x),
    se     = round(sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)), 2))
})

In the output, n is the sample size, mean is the mean, and sd is the standard deviation. The values are rounded to 2 decimal places, which matches the rounding used on WebAssign.

Hint: these commands also appear in your handouts. For a single variable, see the Single Sample t Test handout, section “Some Summary Statistics.” That handout finds the statistics one at a time with separate commands (summary() for the mean, sd() for the standard deviation, and length() for the sample size) instead of the single c() command shown above; either approach gives the same values, but remember to round to 2 decimal places. For a variable broken down by group, see the Independent t Test or One-Way ANOVA and Post-Hoc Tests handout, section “More Advanced Code for Summary Statistics,” which uses the same by() command shown above.

  1. Single sample \(t\) test. Perform a one-tailed single sample \(t\) test on Collaboration to determine whether the mean is significantly greater than a benchmark (null) value of 3.5.

    Hint: see the Single Sample t-Test handout, section “One Sample t Test.” Read the entire section if you do not remember how to test whether a mean is significantly greater than the null value.

  2. Single sample \(t\) test. Perform a one-tailed single sample \(t\) test on Safe_online_practices to determine whether the mean is significantly less than a benchmark (null) value of 3.

    Hint: see the Single Sample t-Test handout, section “One Sample t Test.” Read the entire section if you do not remember how to test whether a mean is significantly less than the null value.

  3. Independent \(t\) test. Perform a two-tailed independent \(t\) test on SearchInternet by Gender to determine whether there is any significant difference between the mean ratings of men and women (a null value of 0). Because of the way the groups are coded in the data set, men are population 1 and women are population 2.

    Run Levene’s test for homogeneity of variance first. Then use its result to choose the correct version of the \(t\) test (equal variances assumed or equal variances not assumed).

    Hint: see the Independent t Test handout, section “Test for Homogeneity (Equality) of Variance,” for Levene’s test, and the rest of the handout for the \(t\) test. Levene’s test uses the car package, which is loaded in the first 45 lines of the Starter Code. See step v of Getting Started if you need to install it.

  4. One-way ANOVA with Tukey’s HSD. Perform a one-way ANOVA on Online_shopping using Income as the factor. Then perform a Tukey’s HSD post-hoc analysis to identify any significant pairwise differences. Run the post-hoc analysis even if the ANOVA is not significant.

    Hint: see the One-Way ANOVA and Post-Hoc Tests handout, sections “One-Way ANOVA Test” and “Post-Hoc Analysis.”

  5. One-way ANOVA with Bonferroni-adjusted LSD. Perform a one-way ANOVA on WordProcessing using Education as the factor. Then perform a Bonferroni-adjusted LSD post-hoc analysis to identify any significant pairwise differences. Run the post-hoc analysis even if the ANOVA is not significant.

    Hint: see the One-Way ANOVA and Post-Hoc Tests handout, sections “One-Way ANOVA Test” and “Post-Hoc Analysis.”

  6. One-way ANOVA with unadjusted Fisher’s LSD. Perform a one-way ANOVA on Total_Percent_Score using Age as the factor. Then perform an unadjusted Fisher’s LSD post-hoc analysis to identify any significant pairwise differences. Run the post-hoc analysis even if the ANOVA is not significant.

    Hint: see the One-Way ANOVA and Post-Hoc Tests handout, sections “One-Way ANOVA Test” and “Post-Hoc Analysis.”

Compiling Your Report

When your code is complete, compile your report and upload it to Canvas. The compiled report shows each piece of your code followed by the output it produced, so it is easy to see which output came from which code. Your compiled report is worth points toward your grade on the R Coding Project.

Any error in your R Script file will stop R from compiling your report. If your file has an error, you must fix it or delete the line of code that causes it. If you are having trouble compiling your report, this short video covers some common problems: Hints for Compiling a Report.

If you are using a personal computer and your report will not compile, check whether you pasted the instructions for installing the car package into your script file. R cannot compile installation code. Delete those lines from your file and then compile it.

Follow these steps to create and submit your report.

  1. From the File menu, select “Compile Report…”.
  2. Choose HTML as the output format. RStudio may ask to install some packages; click “Yes” and let it install what it needs.
  3. Once the packages are installed, the report is created and saved automatically in the same folder as your R Script file.
  4. Your compiled report has the .html extension. In File Explorer, it may show a Chrome or Microsoft Edge icon. This .html file is the file you upload to Canvas.
  5. If you want to view the report from Google Drive in a Chrome browser, download it first and then open it. If you open it directly in a browser tab, it will display as unreadable code.

Use your compiled report to answer the questions in the R Coding Project, Digital Literacy in South Bend assignment on WebAssign. The answers may come from any part of your report; the questions do not necessarily follow the order of your output.
